name: Keel Cloud
title: Give AI useful tools. Let us look after the hosting.
what: A proposed hosted service for the keel toolkit. It connects AI apps to business tools, applies permission rules and keeps those tools running for the team.
why: Building tools is only part of the job. Businesses also need hosting, updates, access controls and records of what happened.
outcome: Less infrastructure to manage, reusable tools and more control over what AI assistants can do.
example: A business connects its booking system and help desk. The AI can look up a trip, but must ask a person before changing it.
note: Keel Cloud is a proposed paid service built on the open-source keel toolkit. Cloud pricing is indicative.

name: ATFGraph Cloud
title: Run AI agents without running the servers.
what: A proposed hosted service that runs and monitors AI agents, saves their progress and lets them wait for an update or approval before continuing.
why: Business tasks can last days. Teams need reliable hosting, a record of progress and a way to restart work after an interruption.
outcome: Less server management, more reliable work over time and a clear view of running, waiting and completed jobs.
example: An agent checks a request on Monday, waits for a manager’s approval and continues on Thursday with its progress saved.
note: ATFGraph Cloud is the proposed managed service for the open-source ATFGraph engine. Cloud pricing is indicative.

name: ctx.travel
title: A travel helper that remembers you—and looks for savings.
what: An app that turns saved videos, places and booking emails into a trip. It finds member prices, books with approval and watches for eligible price drops.
why: Planning means juggling apps, emails and tabs. Most booking sites stop helping once the purchase is done.
outcome: Less effort to plan, choices that fit the traveller and possible savings before and after booking.
example: Save a Tokyo food video. ctx adds the place to your plan, finds a nearby hotel and keeps checking its price.
note: Savings depend on availability and booking rules; a stated share of price-drop savings goes to ctx.

name: mcpx.travel
role: For AI app builders + travel sellers
title: Turn an AI travel conversation into a real booking.
what: One software connection gives AI apps tools to find flights, stays and activities, hold an offer, book it and manage later changes.
why: An app can recommend a trip without being able to book it. Connecting suppliers, payments and aftercare is a large job.
outcome: A faster route to launching travel products and earning from bookings, with less connection work.
example: A travel chat app uses mcpx to show flights, hold the chosen fare and confirm the trip after the customer approves.
note: mcpx provides booking tools. ADN proposes the shared market where buyers and sellers make deals.

name: Agentic TMS-CRM
title: An assistant for every advisor. Care for every trip.
what: Customer records and trip management in one place. A personal AI agent remembers each client, prepares their trip, books with approval and keeps watching for changes.
why: Enquiries, notes and bookings sit in different places. Advisors lose time copying details and chasing the next task.
outcome: Less admin, more time with customers and a clearer view of every trip from first enquiry to home again.
example: Maya asks for a quiet beach break. Her agent remembers what she likes, prepares a trip and asks the advisor to approve it.
note: The agent works within the advisor’s rules and asks before booking or payment.

name: Portal
title: Reach the suppliers that still book by website or message.
what: A booking helper that uses supplier websites with permission. For operators without a system, it can arrange a booking by message or phone and keep a tidy record.
why: Staff often type the same names again, chase a reply and copy a confirmation into another system.
outcome: Less repeated work and more local suppliers available to sell, without asking each operator to buy new software.
example: A boat operator takes bookings on WhatsApp. The helper asks for two seats and records the operator’s confirmation.
note: Supplier permission comes first. A person approves spending.

name: Visa clearance
title: Get the paperwork ready before the traveller leaves.
what: An AI helper checks which visas and entry papers a trip needs, prepares forms and tracks the application. A trained person reviews it before it is sent.
why: A booked flight does not mean a traveller has permission to enter. Finding missing papers late can put the whole trip at risk.
outcome: Less form-filling for teams, clearer next steps for travellers and fewer last-minute paperwork surprises.
example: A photo is missing from an application. The helper flags it early, so the traveller can supply it before the review.
note: Governments decide on visas and entry. Approval cannot be guaranteed.

name: ADN + Exchange
title: Ask once. Let trusted travel suppliers compete for the trip.
what: A proposed market where AI buyers request travel and suppliers reply with private offers. Shared rules cover who can trade, payments and problems.
why: Every buyer currently needs separate supplier connections and agreements. Suppliers need to know who is asking and what they can buy.
outcome: Less setup for buyers and sellers, more choice and a clear record of what each side agreed.
example: An agent asks for a Tokyo hotel. Hotels offer rooms privately, and one agrees to include breakfast within the traveller’s budget.
note: This is a proposal; members, payment arrangements and fees are still to be agreed.

name: Voice & Concierge
role: For hotels, holiday stays + travel teams
title: A warm welcome, even when your team is busy.
what: An AI receptionist that answers calls and messages, helps with everyday guest requests and keeps staff informed in one shared inbox.
why: Guests need help after hours and during busy periods. Missed calls and scattered messages create extra work and lost enquiries.
outcome: Fewer missed enquiries, quicker answers and more staff time for guests who need a person. These are the aims of a future pilot.
example: A guest calls at 2am about a late arrival. The assistant explains the approved arrival process and prepares a note for reception.
note: Incubating: an early business concept and interactive preview. Live phone, messaging and booking connections are not yet active.
